9.5.3. Inadvertent Unblinding
Every effort will be made to blind both the patient and the investigator to the identity of the
treatment, but the inadvertent unblinding of a patient may occur. A double-blind study design is
known to be imperfect in the oncolytic setting because the potential for individual unblinding
exists due to treatment-related signs and symptoms. If an investigator, site personnel performing
assessments, or patient is unblinded, the unblinding will not be sufficient cause (in and of itself)
for that patient to be discontinued from study therapy or excluded from any safety or efficacy
analyses.

patients to continue on study treatment in the event of unblinding, the investigator must obtain
specific approval from a Lilly CRP for the patient to continue in the study.

12. Sample Size and Statistical Methods
12.1. Determination of Sample Size
The primary objective of this study is to compare abemaciclib plus fulvestrant versus placebo
plus fulvestrant in terms of PFS for women with HR+, HER2- locally advanced or metastatic
breast cancer.
This study will enroll 2 strata of patients according to prior endocrine therapy: endocrine
therapy pretreated (EP) patients and endocrine therapy naïve (EN) patients.
The primary statistical analyses will be performed on patients in the EP stratum.
The initial study protocol specified an enrollment of 450 EP patients. Amendment (a) changed
the starting dose of blinded study drug from 200 mg Q12H to 150 mg Q12H. In addition to
describing the safety profile in the full EP safety population, safety analyses will be conducted in
the subgroup of patients enrolled under Amendment (a) with a starting dose of 150 mg Q12H. In
order to do this robustly, enrollment to the study will continue until 450 EP patients are enrolled
at a starting dose of 150 mg Q12H. As of the implementation of Amendment (a), approximately
180 EP patients had been enrolled at a starting dose of 200 mg Q12H. Including these 180
patients, the final size of the EP stratum will be approximately 450 + 180 = 630 patients.
Patients will be randomized in a 2:1 ratio using the following stratification factors: nature of
disease (visceral metastases versus bone only metastases versus other) and sensitivity to
endocrine therapy (primary resistance versus secondary resistance).
A 2-look group-sequential design of the primary endpoint will be used to accommodate an
event-driven plan for the interim and final PFS analyses (see Section 12.2.7 for details). The
final PFS analysis will be performed after 378 PFS events have occurred in the EP stratum (that
is, a 40% censoring rate). Assuming a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.703, this sample size yields
approximately 90% statistical power to detect superiority of the abemaciclib plus fulvestrant arm
over the placebo plus fulvestrant arm with the use of a 1-sided log-rank test and a type I error of
0.025. If the true median PFS for the placebo plus fulvestrant arm is 6.5 months, then the HR of
0.703 amounts to an approximately 2.75-month (42%) improvement in median PFS for the
abemaciclib plus fulvestrant arm under an additional assumption of exponential survival
distribution.
OS is an important secondary endpoint for this study. OS will be tested only if the test of PFS is
significant. The final OS analysis will be conducted at 441 OS events in the EP stratum (see
Section 12.2.8 for details).

12.2.8.2. Objective Response Rate, DCR, CBR, and DoR
The objective response rate, DCR, and CBR of each treatment arm will be calculated as defined
in Section 10.1.4 using the ITT population. All rates will be compared between treatment arms
based on a normal approximation for the difference between the rates.
The DoR time is defined only for responders (patients with a best response of CR or PR). It is
measured from the date of first evidence of CR or PR to the date of objective progression or the
date of death due to any cause, whichever is earlier. A Kaplan-Meier analysis of DoR will be
performed to estimate the DoR curve for each arm.

24|MONARCH 2 was a global, double-blind, phase III study of women with hormone receptor-positive
25|and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-negative ABC who had progressed while receiving

33|Between August 2014 and December 2015, 669 patients were randomly assigned to receive
34|abemaciclib plus fulvestrant (n = 446) or placebo plus fulvestrant (n = 223). Abemaciclib plus ful-
35|vestrant significantly extended PFS versus fulvestrant alone (median, 16.4 v 9.3 months; hazard

40|22.9%), and fatigue (39.9% v 26.9%).

43|ORR and demonstrating a tolerable safety profile in women with hormone receptor-positive and
44|human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-negative ABC who progressed while receiving ET.

14|Statistical Analysis
15|The study was designed to compare the PFS for abemaciclib plus
16|fulvestrant to that for placebo plus fulvestrant. The study initially planned
17|to enroll 450 patients into the intent-to-treat (ITT) population. However,
18|after a change in the starting dose of the blinded-study drug from 200 mg
19|to 150 mg, the sample size was increased to 630 patients to ensure at least
20|450 patients were enrolled at the 150-mg dose. The primary statistical
21|analyses for investigator-assessed PFS were performed on the ITT pop-
22|ulation, which included all patients regardless of starting dose. Sensitivity
23|analyses were planned that (1) included only patients enrolled after the
24|change in starting dose and that (2) determined progression on the basis of
25|a blinded, independent central review.
26|The primary end point, investigator-assessed PFS, was evaluated using
27|a log-rank test stratified by metastatic site and ET resistance. The final
28|analysis was planned at 378 PFS events, which would provide approximately
29|90% power assuming a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.703 at a one-sided a of 0.025,
30|which corresponds to a 2.75-month improvement over the true median PFS
31|for the control arm of 6.5 months.22 One efficacy interim analysis was
32|planned to be at 70% of the final PFS events. The a control for the secondary
33|end point of OS was maintained using a hierarchical testing approach.
34|The odds ratio estimator and the stratified Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel
35|test were used to compare the rates of binary end points. Two-sided
36|P values were used to compare efficacy between treatment groups and for
37|interaction tests associated with the subgroup factors. An exploratory
38|mixed-model analysis was used to compare change in tumor size over time.
39|Unless otherwise noted, all hypothesis tests were performed at the two-
40|sided .05 level, and all confidence intervals used a 95% confidence level.
41|Safety was assessed in all patients who received at least one dose of study
42|drug (ie, the safety population). SAS (version 9.2 or later; SAS Institute,
43|Cary, NC) was used for statistical analyses.

5|DISCUSSION
6|The MONARCH 2 study demonstrated that abemaciclib, a
7|potent CDK 4 and 6 inhibitor dosed on a continuous schedule,
8|significantly extended PFS when added to fulvestrant in women
9|with HR+/ HER2-ABC whose disease had progressed while
10|they were receiving ET. This benefit was consistent across
11|subgroups.
12|MONARCH 2 evaluated patients whose disease progressed
13|while they were receiving neoadjuvant or adjuvant ET, # 12 months
14|after adjuvant ET, or while receiving ET for ABC. Only 8.8% of
15|patients progressed within 12 months after completing adjuvant
16|therapy. Patients could not have received chemotherapy or more
17|than one line of ET for mBC, making this a more homogeneous
18|population than in previous studies of patients whose disease
19|progressed while they were receiving prior ET for ABC.5,22,24-26
20|The MONARCH 2 population is readily identifiable in the clinical
21|setting. To the best of our knowledge, the median PFS of
22|16.4 months and the 7.2-month improvement over control
23|therapy observed in patients who received abemaciclib plus
24|fulvestrant represents the longest reported in a population with
25|ABC whose disease had progressed while they were receiving
26|prior ET.5,22,24-26
27|It is not typical for ET-based treatments to induce sub-
28|stantial tumor shrinkage, especially in patients whose disease
29|has progressed while they were receiving prior ET.27 The ad-
30|dition of abemaciclib to fulvestrant significantly improved
31|ORR, which included 14 patients in the abemaciclib arm ex-
32|periencing a CR. Tumor size reduction was more pronounced
33|in the abemaciclib arm, and tumor response was durable (Fig
34|4). To the best of our knowledge, the ORR achieved in patients
35|who received abemaciclib plus fulvestrant is the highest ob-
36|served in a phase III study of patients whose disease had

1|The safety profile of abemaciclib with fulvestrant was broadly
2|consistent with that reported for other CDK 4 and 6 inhibitors,5,6
3|with the exception of diarrhea. Most diarrhea was of low grade,
4|occurred early in the first treatment cycle, and was managed with
5|dose adjustment and standard antidiarrheal medication. Other
6|frequent, nonhematological AEs in the abemaciclib arm included
7|nausea, fatigue, and abdominal pain. Severe neutropenia has been
8|frequently reported in phase III studies with other CDK 4 and 6
9|inhibitors and was a dose-limiting toxicity leading to the definition
10|of intermittent dosing schedules.5,6,28,29 This has not been the case
11|in MONARCH 2 and other studies of abemaciclib, in which severe
12|neutropenia has been infrequent.4,10,30 This may be due to the
13|greater relative potency of abemaciclib for cyclin D1/CDK4
14|compared with cyclin D3/CDK6 observed in cell-free enzymatic
15|assays.16
16|In conclusion, MONARCH 2, an evaluation for abemaciclib
17|given at a dosage of 150 mg twice daily on a continuous schedule
18|in combination with fulvestrant, significantly improved PFS and
19|ORR compared with placebo plus fulvestrant and showed a tol-
20|erable safety profile in patients with HR+/HER2-ABC whose
21|disease had progressed while they were receiving prior ET.
22|Abemaciclib plus fulvestrant was an effective treatment for pa-
23|tients with HR+/HER2-ABC whose disease progressed while
24|they were receiving ET.

6|Using an interactive, web-based randomization scheme, patients were

6|Outcomes
7|The primary end point, investigator-assessed PFS, was analyzed from
8|the time of random assignment until objective PD or death for any reason.
9|Key secondary end points included objective response rate (ORR; ie,
10|proportion of patients with CR or PR), duration of response (time from
11|CR or PR until PD or death), CBR, and safety and tolerability. Other
12|secondary end points not reported in this analysis are overall survival (OS),
13|quality of life measures, and pharmacokinetics.
14|Statistical Analysis
15|The study was designed to compare the PFS for abemaciclib plus
16|fulvestrant to that for placebo plus fulvestrant. The study initially planned
17|to enroll 450 patients into the intent-to-treat (ITT) population. However,
18|after a change in the starting dose of the blinded-study drug from 200 mg
19|to 150 mg, the sample size was increased to 630 patients to ensure at least
20|450 patients were enrolled at the 150-mg dose. The primary statistical
21|analyses for investigator-assessed PFS were performed on the ITT pop-
22|ulation, which included all patients regardless of starting dose. Sensitivity
23|analyses were planned that (1) included only patients enrolled after the
24|change in starting dose and that (2) determined progression on the basis of
25|a blinded, independent central review.

14|Statistical Analysis
15|The study was designed to compare the PFS for abemaciclib plus
16|fulvestrant to that for placebo plus fulvestrant. The study initially planned
17|to enroll 450 patients into the intent-to-treat (ITT) population. However,
18|after a change in the starting dose of the blinded-study drug from 200 mg
19|to 150 mg, the sample size was increased to 630 patients to ensure at least
20|450 patients were enrolled at the 150-mg dose. The primary statistical
21|analyses for investigator-assessed PFS were performed on the ITT pop-
22|ulation, which included all patients regardless of starting dose. Sensitivity
23|analyses were planned that (1) included only patients enrolled after the
24|change in starting dose and that (2) determined progression on the basis of
25|a blinded, independent central review.
26|The primary end point, investigator-assessed PFS, was evaluated using
27|a log-rank test stratified by metastatic site and ET resistance. The final
28|analysis was planned at 378 PFS events, which would provide approximately
29|90% power assuming a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.703 at a one-sided a of 0.025,
30|which corresponds to a 2.75-month improvement over the true median PFS
31|for the control arm of 6.5 months.22 One efficacy interim analysis was
32|planned to be at 70% of the final PFS events. The a control for the secondary
33|end point of OS was maintained using a hierarchical testing approach.
34|The odds ratio estimator and the stratified Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel
35|test were used to compare the rates of binary end points. Two-sided
36|P values were used to compare efficacy between treatment groups and for
37|interaction tests associated with the subgroup factors. An exploratory
38|mixed-model analysis was used to compare change in tumor size over time.
39|Unless otherwise noted, all hypothesis tests were performed at the two-
40|sided .05 level, and all confidence intervals used a 95% confidence level.
41|Safety was assessed in all patients who received at least one dose of study
42|drug (ie, the safety population). SAS (version 9.2 or later; SAS Institute,
43|Cary, NC) was used for statistical analyses.

5|DISCUSSION
6|The MONARCH 2 study demonstrated that abemaciclib, a
7|potent CDK 4 and 6 inhibitor dosed on a continuous schedule,
8|significantly extended PFS when added to fulvestrant in women
9|with HR+/ HER2-ABC whose disease had progressed while
10|they were receiving ET. This benefit was consistent across
11|subgroups.
12|MONARCH 2 evaluated patients whose disease progressed
13|while they were receiving neoadjuvant or adjuvant ET, # 12 months
14|after adjuvant ET, or while receiving ET for ABC. Only 8.8% of
15|patients progressed within 12 months after completing adjuvant
16|therapy. Patients could not have received chemotherapy or more
17|than one line of ET for mBC, making this a more homogeneous
18|population than in previous studies of patients whose disease
19|progressed while they were receiving prior ET for ABC.5,22,24-26
20|The MONARCH 2 population is readily identifiable in the clinical
21|setting. To the best of our knowledge, the median PFS of
22|16.4 months and the 7.2-month improvement over control
23|therapy observed in patients who received abemaciclib plus
24|fulvestrant represents the longest reported in a population with

1|The safety profile of abemaciclib with fulvestrant was broadly
2|consistent with that reported for other CDK 4 and 6 inhibitors,5,6
3|with the exception of diarrhea. Most diarrhea was of low grade,
4|occurred early in the first treatment cycle, and was managed with
5|dose adjustment and standard antidiarrheal medication. Other
6|frequent, nonhematological AEs in the abemaciclib arm included
7|nausea, fatigue, and abdominal pain. Severe neutropenia has been
8|frequently reported in phase III studies with other CDK 4 and 6
9|inhibitors and was a dose-limiting toxicity leading to the definition
10|of intermittent dosing schedules.5,6,28,29 This has not been the case
11|in MONARCH 2 and other studies of abemaciclib, in which severe
12|neutropenia has been infrequent.4,10,30 This may be due to the
13|greater relative potency of abemaciclib for cyclin D1/CDK4
14|compared with cyclin D3/CDK6 observed in cell-free enzymatic
15|assays.16
16|In conclusion, MONARCH 2, an evaluation for abemaciclib
17|given at a dosage of 150 mg twice daily on a continuous schedule
18|in combination with fulvestrant, significantly improved PFS and
19|ORR compared with placebo plus fulvestrant and showed a tol-
20|erable safety profile in patients with HR+/HER2-ABC whose
21|disease had progressed while they were receiving prior ET.
22|Abemaciclib plus fulvestrant was an effective treatment for pa-
23|tients with HR+/HER2-ABC whose disease progressed while
24|they were receiving ET.

Investigational treatment administration in this study is double-blind; that is, patients,

9.5.3. Inadvertent Unblinding
Every effort will be made to blind both the patient and the investigator to the identity of the
treatment, but the inadvertent unblinding of a patient may occur. A double-blind study design is
known to be imperfect in the oncolytic setting because the potential for individual unblinding
exists due to treatment-related signs and symptoms. If an investigator, site personnel performing
assessments, or patient is unblinded, the unblinding will not be sufficient cause (in and of itself)
for that patient to be discontinued from study therapy or excluded from any safety or efficacy
analyses.
Additionally, there may be ethical reasons to have the patient remain on the study treatment. For
patients to continue on study treatment in the event of unblinding, the investigator must obtain
specific approval from a Lilly CRP for the patient to continue in the study.

12.2. Statistical and Analytical Plans
12.2.1. Analysis Populations
The ITT population will be comprised of all randomized patients randomized within the EP
strata (either primary endocrine resistance or secondary endocrine resistance), per IWRS.
The safety population will include all randomized EP patients who receive at least one dose of
any study drug.
Patients randomized within the 'no prior endocrine therapy' stratum comprise the EN population.
Exploratory efficacy analyses will be performed on this population. The EN safety population
will include all randomized EN patients who receive at least one dose of any study drug.
12.2.2. General Considerations
Statistical analysis of this study will be the responsibility of Lilly.
Primary statistical analyses will be conducted on the ITT population, as defined in
Section 12.2.1. Analyses will be performed based on the treatment group to which patients were
randomized (regardless of which treatment was received).

12.2. Statistical and Analytical Plans
12.2.1. Analysis Populations
The ITT population will be comprised of all randomized patients randomized within the EP
strata (either primary endocrine resistance or secondary endocrine resistance), per IWRS.
The safety population will include all randomized EP patients who receive at least one dose of
any study drug.
Patients randomized within the 'no prior endocrine therapy' stratum comprise the EN population.
Exploratory efficacy analyses will be performed on this population. The EN safety population
will include all randomized EN patients who receive at least one dose of any study drug.
12.2.2. General Considerations
Statistical analysis of this study will be the responsibility of Lilly.
Primary statistical analyses will be conducted on the ITT population, as defined in
Section 12.2.1. Analyses will be performed based on the treatment group to which patients were
randomized (regardless of which treatment was received).

answers.justification: The approved primary PFS result is the protocol-defined ITT cohort in the endocrine-resistant (EP) strata (669 participants); the 44 endocrine-naïve participants formed a separate exploratory EN stratum and are not missing outcomes from this primary cohort. In the EP cohort, the flow diagram reports only 6 of 446 and 4 of 223 lost to follow-up (10/669, about 1.5%). It separately reports treatment discontinuation, which does not itself mean PFS follow-up stopped. The protocol states that tumor assessments continued after treatment discontinuation until progression or final PFS analysis, and defines censoring for loss to follow-up at the last adequate tumor assessment. This supports outcome availability for nearly all participants in the approved primary-result population, although reporting does not give a complete arm-specific breakdown of administrative versus loss-related censoring.
unknowns: The main article does not describe follow-up status for each participant or distinguish the 10 losses from administrative censoring in the Kaplan–Meier analysis.
The protocol-defined EP population is the primary PFS population; the separate EN stratum's exploratory efficacy results are not part of the selected primary Result.

The protocol identifies these participants as a separate EN stratum, rather than as participants with missing outcome data in the primary EP analysis.

Tumors were measured by computed tomography or magnetic
resonance imaging according to RECIST version 1.1 within 28 days before
random assignment (baseline) and then every 8 weeks the first year, every
12 weeks thereafter, and within 2 weeks of clinical progression. Patients
underwent bone scintigraphy at baseline, and then again every sixth cycle
starting with cycle 7. Hematologic and blood chemistry laboratory tests
were performed centrally on days 1 and 15 of the first cycle and day 1 of all
remaining cycles.

Outcomes
The primary end point, investigator-assessed PFS, was analyzed from
the time of random assignment until objective PD or death for any reason.

investigational sites, and the sponsor study team do not have immediate access to treatment
assignments for any patients. This design feature minimizes potential bias due to knowledge of
patient's treatment during evaluation of study endpoints, at the patient level or aggregated across
patients.
